utterances.text: As far as I can remember, starting from the 15th of June, this vehicle was providing citizens with the information over the megaphone in the zone controlled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to refer you to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Your Honour, before I ask this question, if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In your statement, Witness 144, you refer to various meetings with Zdravko Samardzija. You refer to a meeting with Komljenovic was present. That's at paragraph 108. You refer to his presence at the police station. That's paragraph 114. And you refer to him ordering confinement at paragraph 119. Can you describe to the Court who Zdravko Samardzija was and what his role in Kotor Varos was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: I saw Zdravko Samardzija for the first time several days after the outbreak of clashes in Kotor Varos, when he came with Tomjenovic [phoen] to Kotor Varos, to Cepak, where he stated his full name and he said that he was a lawyer and worked at the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, and that the residents of Cepak were supposed to hand over their weapons and that nothing would happen to them, that the process would be carried out quickly and that life would return to normal in Kotor Varos. The second encounter was the one I just described, when I was given a permit for the freedom of movement by him. The third encounter with Zdravko Samardzija was on the occasion of my second arrest, when I was arrested and taken to the police station. It was then that I realised that Zdravko Samardzija was in command of all the Special Forces, special police forces that were present in the area. As I was being taken out of the truck that took me there, because a truck took me from my home, because I had again returned home, and that was the next time I saw Zdravko Samardzija again. And he asked me, "Well, what are you doing here?" His subordinate, Nenad Kajkut, grabbed me by my hair, the back of my hair, and hit me in the head very strongly. Then he took me into the police station, to the first room on the right. There were several other detainees standing in the corridor with their backs facing the wall. They were actually -- the palms of their hands were leaning against the wall, just with three fingers stretched out. They took me into this room, where I saw two members of the Serb Special Forces. They started beating me, and it went on for hours. Amidst the beating and the strikes, they kept asking me about my colleagues from the SDA, about what I knew about them, what I knew about the neighbours who left their homes and took to the woods. This went on for hours. At a certain point, Zdravko Samardzija appeared at the doorstep and told the other two - one of them was Ostoja Verbica [phoen], the other Danko Kajkut. I learnt their names later on. I did not know them from before. Samardzija told them, "Don't kill him. I need limb alive because I need to interrogate him." They continued beating me upon Samardzija's departure. In some 15 minutes, the doors opened again and Zdravko Samardzija appeared holding a pistol in his hand, pointed the pistol at them and said, "Did you hear what I said? I need him alive." And he went out again. I saw Samardzija Zdravko once again the following day, or rather, I failed to say that on that same day at 10.00 in the evening, Zdravko Samardzija took us to a room that was that same solitary cell where they locked me the first time. Now there were 17 people in that room that was of an area of maybe 1 by 1.5 metres. There was no air there, because there were only a few holes in the wall. We started suffocating and banging against the door. Later on they transferred us to an office in the police station, where we spent the night. Zdravko Samardzija told us, "You will spend the night here and then we'll see what we're going to do with you tomorrow." The following day, we spent the whole day standing in front of the police station under an awning that was basically a parking place for a police vehicle. I had the opportunity of seeing many Serbs from Kotor Varos, including Zdravko Samardzija, who kept entering and leaving the building, whereas the members of the Special Forces who were in command of Zdravko Samardzija would come, approach us, beat us, and then go away, return, beat us again. And this was an eternal day of suffering for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, could I just stop you there. You stated that the Special Forces were under the command of Samardzija. Whilst you were detained in the school, following your detention in the police station, and whilst you were detained in the prison, subsequent to your detention in the school, did you see Samardzija or did you see the members of the Special Forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: The members of the Special Forces came to the school where we were detained and to the prison when I was subsequently transferred there. Zdravko Samardzija came only in the first couple of days. Later on, we didn't see him any more. One of the guards, we knew these guards because these guards used to be our workmates, we learnt from them that Zdravko Samardzija went to Jajce, the town of Jajce, and Zdravko Samardzija's role was taken by Slobodan Dubocanin. Slobodan Dubocanin frequently came to the school where we were detained, accompanied by several members of the Special Forces, calling out individuals into the corridor to beat them, including myself. And this went on for two months, for the duration of our detention at the school, the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were detained at the police station, you referred to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry. Microphone is now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you were detained at the police station, you referred to several other detainees. What was the nationality of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: The first day, the first time I was taken to the police station, that was on the 7th of July, I saw several persons in the corridor who were also brought in, who were ethnic Croats, and there were also two Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, I'd like to present the next two exhibits to the witness. They're the conclusion on resettlement dated 18 June 1992, and the statement of Safet Smajlovic dated 21 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit numbers P339 and P340.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, the document dated 18 June 1992 is a conclusion of the Crisis Staff of Kotor Varos, and it refers to arrangement for the resettlement of Rasim Mehmedovic to Zagreb through the resettlement agency. Did you know Rasim Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did he leave Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When did you first hear of the resettlement agency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: I heard when the vehicle drove by, that I described before, where there was a PA system mounted, saying that all citizens of Croat and Muslim ethnicity who wished to leave Kotor Varos municipality and had done nothing against the Serb people were free to do so by registering with the Red Cross office. This was probably a reference to this agency. But I was not familiar with the existence of this specific agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What was the nationality of Rasim Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to the next document, dated 21 August 1992, which is a statement from Safet Smajlovic in relation to his departure from Kotor Varos. And it states at the second substantial paragraph, under the numbered points 1 to 11: "I wish to move away and I leave behind my land in Kotor and my destroyed house." And then states that he's taking with him various members of his family. Did you hear, as at August 1992, about conditions that may have been imposed on those that wished to leave Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: During that period of time, and specifically, on the 21st of August, I was in detention. But before I was detained, I had heard of people who wished to do just that, and they had to get themselves registered, and the condition imposed was that they voluntarily hand over all their property to the Serbian Republic. And they were supposed to leave the key to their flat or house at the centre to which they were supposed to report. And they had to cover the transport charges as far as wherever it was that they wished to go. In 99 per cent of the cases, the destination was Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you know Safet Smajlovic, and if so, do you know what nationality he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. He is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'd like to proceed to the next exhibit, Your Honour, which is a document dated 19 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P341.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness 144, this document before you is an extract from the minutes of the 26th session of the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff held on 19 June 1992. In the second -- in the first item, in the second paragraph, there is information provided by Mane Tepic as follows: "He informed the Crisis Staff on yesterday's activities by units that are in the Kotor Varos area and pointed out that the Rujika had been cleaned out and taken yesterday, that a soldier from the village of Tesic had been captured and taken away and that six soldiers had been surrounded because they had not retreated in time." Do you have any information about events that took place in June 1992 in Rujika?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Rujika, I mean the place, is at a distance of about 500 or 600 metres from my house, as the crow flies. Therefore, standing at the window of my house, I could see clearly what was going on over there. In those days, I saw that an attack had been carried out, very similar to the one that had been launched against Cepak. And now it was Rujika. There was a blue APC with "police" written on it and it was used by special police forces to enter the Rujika area, or rather, Kotoriste. Allow me to explain, to be more specific about this. There is a hillock behind the hotel in Kotor Varos, and the name of that hillock is Rujika. Behind that hillock, or mound, which was a favourite weekend destination in town, there is another neighbourhood that belongs to the town, and this neighbourhood is called Kotoriste. I could see clearly that some people were being taken out of their houses, that some houses had been set fire to, and that some of the inhabitants of Kotoriste had probably fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, can I just interrupt you for a moment. Was Kotoriste a Muslim or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: It was a Croat village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to move to the next exhibit, and that is document dated 21st June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P342.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This exhibit is an extract from the minutes of the 31st meeting of the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to refer you to the last paragraph under the heading "item 2," where it states: "It was concluded that Savo should invite Ljuban or Zdravko to the next Crisis Staff meeting and he was then given the task of briefing Stojan Z on problems we are experiencing and scheduling a meeting, attendance at which should be ensured from the following persons in addition to KS members: Brdjanin, Peulic, Zupljanin, and other competent people who might be able to help the KS in addressing these problems." From the context of that paragraph, are you able to identify who Savo, Ljuban, and Zdravko were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: I can assume that it is Savo Tepic. As for Ljuban, this could be a reference to Ljuban Ecim, who was a member of a special police unit, alongside with Slobodan Dubocanin, and he would come to the prison very often while we were detained at the school building. The third person could have been Zdravko Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When Ljuban Ecim came to the school building, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: He was usually not alone. He would usually have several members of the Special Forces with him. They would take prisoners out, question them, beat them, and then send them back to their cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to proceed to the next exhibit, which is a document dated 24 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 343.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This document is the extract from the minutes of the 36th session of the Crisis Staff, held on 24 June 1992. I note that in the introductory paragraph it refers to the presence of Inspector Pejic, and under item 3, it states that Inspector Pejic informed the Crisis Staff about the work of the security service and the results of the questioning of the persons who had been brought in. Witness 144, do you know who this Inspector Pejic is, and if so, when did you either meet with him or see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Inspector Pejic is Zdravko Pejic. A long time ago he used to work with the Kotor Varos SUP ministry of the secretariat of the interior. He worked on the issuing of identity cards and travel documents. He was then promoted and became inspector of the social security services. I can't be sure when, but it was probably 1980-something that he retired. Following the outbreak of clashes in Kotor Varos, he was appointed inspector with the public security station in Kotor Varos, and his authority was far superior to that of other inspectors. He was the one who interrogated prisoners. He was the one who approved their detention or release. He would take them away for interrogation, along with other police officers. The police officers would beat them, and meanwhile, he would interrogate them. While he was at the prison, I met him. I can't give you the exact number of times, but certainly very many times, once a week, at least, probably even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did the guards ever say anything to you in respect of Zdravko Pejic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Yes. The guards used to tell us that our fate hinged on Zdravko Pejic. He took part in the negotiations for exchanges when prisoners were exchanged, as well as the last one, when we were eventually exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present to the witness the next two exhibits. One is dated 26 June 1992, and the other is a lengthy document, headed "list of camp prisoners in Kotor Varos from 11 June 1992 onwards."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document will be Prosecution Exhibit number P344, and the second document, P345.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness 144, first of all, I'd like to refer you to the lengthy list. Is this a list that you prepared; and if so, can you describe to the Court when you prepared it and what it describes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Yes. This is a list of prisoners in the elementary school prison, as well as the prison behind the court building. I was the one who drew it up. It contains the names of persons who were detained in those prisons that I was familiar with. I produced this list following my release, or rather, once I had been exchanged and taken to a transit centre in Karlovac, Croatia. All the names from Kotor Varos, from the centre, from Cepak, from Kotoriste, from Kukavica, from Donja Varos, all these names were recorded by myself personally. As for the other part, in reference to the village of Vrbanjci, I was assisted by (redacted), people who are actually from that area and were also detained with me in those camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness 144, does this list represent a list of people that were detained and deported from Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What is the nationality of the people on this list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been alerted to the fact that this is a document that we should place under seal, if we can do that. And I apologise for not stating that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, it's tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness 144, I'd like to refer you to the other document that's before you, dated 26 June 1992. And in particular, I'd like to refer you to the entry under item 1 that refers to information from Dr. Gajanin and Nedjeljko Djekanovic, and the information is as follows: Dr. Gajanin -- and just for clarity, this is the extract from the minutes of the 40th session of the Crisis Staff of Kotor Varos on the 26th of June, 1992. Dr. Gajanin informed the Crisis Staff of the situation as regards casualties and reported on what had been done on the premises of the health centre by members of the special unit which he had tried to prevent but was driven away at gunpoint. Nedjeljko Djekanovic said that last night he had told Dubocanin about everything going on at the health centre and in the town and had been assured by him that it would be prevented. He also said that all these questions had to be cleared up and information provided on the behaviour of the members of the special unit at the meeting with S. Zupljanin, the chief of the CSB, scheduled for tomorrow. Zarko Mikic said the Crisis Staff had discussed the behaviour of the members of the special unit on several occasions and were unable to influence them, and he asked Lieutenant Colonel Peulic to help solve this problem." Do you know what happened at the health centre, and if so, can you describe that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: What I know about what happened at the health centre I learned after I had been transferred from the elementary school building to the prison, which occurred in late August. In room 1, which was the room where I was detained, I met some acquaintances of mine, some of whom had witnessed this event on the 25th of June, 1992. It was Enes Terzic and Sevel Djuvelek who were there that told me what happened. A group of Muslims was brought to the health centre from a neighbourhood known as Kukavica. They were brought within the health centre compound, escorted by members of the Serb Special Forces, where they shot a number of them, while others were tortured. Enes showed me his leg. They unleashed a dog on him. The dog bit him and he had deep scars from these dog bites. Sevel Djuvelek told me that his father had been killed there. That was how I learned about that event and what exactly happened at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present to the witness the last two documents I wish to present to him, and they are, firstly, a document dated 30 June 1992; and secondly, a document dated 29 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness 144, the first document I'd like you to look at is the extract from the minutes of the 48th meeting of the Crisis Staff of Kotor Varos, held on 30th of June, 1992. There's a reference to the attendance of Slobodan Dubocanin at this meeting, and the last item on item 1 states that Kajkut is to be assigned to a unit. You have previously mentioned two gentlemen by the name of Kajkut. What unit were they involved with, and what was their relationship to Dubocanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: During my time in detention, I met the Kajkut brothers, Nenad and Danko. Nenad Kajkut had some sort of position of leadership. It is difficult to tell exactly what the hierarchy was, but he was subordinate to Zdravko Samardzija, and later on to Slobodan Dubocanin. Danko Kajkut, on the other hand, was an ordinary member of the Special Forces. He carried out their orders. And most of the time, he was beating us in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were you beaten by Nenad Kajkut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: Yes. The first time he hit me was when I was first brought in, as I've already described. He cracked me over the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You've previously referred to the role of Savo Tepic as the police commander. What was the relationship between Savo Tepic and the special unit commanders Samardzija and Dubocanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: They were all staying at the police station in Kotor Varos. Members of the Special Forces were on the third floor of the police station. And the Serb police, under the leadership of Savo Tepic, were also in the same building, in the same offices where police officers used to be before. There was cooperation between them, and the way I see it, there were two different channels. There were some tasks that were carried out by members of the Special Forces with no control or supervision whatsoever from the ordinary police forces. Whenever we were taken to clean the lavatories of the police station, we would normally be beaten by members of the Special Forces. And whenever a member of the ordinary police forces tried to aid us, they would be driven away, invariably. That is what leads me to conclude that these were two separate formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who was the Special Forces answering to?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, rather than a question in that form, perhaps a question directed to what the witness actually witnessed, as opposed to that sort of generalised question. It's most important, Your Honour, to have the actual observations of the witness as opposed to a question of the nature of who was the Special Forces answering to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, perhaps you'll first ask the witness whether he has any knowledge based on what -- as to hierarchical structures or practices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness 144, did you observe the members of the special units answering to any other authority than that of Dubocanin or Samardzija, and what did you know about the relationship between Dubocanin or Samardzija and other authority figures in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: What I witnessed myself was that Zdravko Samardzija, for as long as he was there, and then later Slobodan Dubocanin, had their own group of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. members of the Special Forces, and they had different clothes that distinguished them from the remaining police units. They had camouflage uniforms. Samardzija Zdravko, Dubocanin Slobodan, Kajkut, Nenad Kajkut, Vrbica and the others had camouflage caps, which was a mark of distinction in relation to their position in the hierarchy while all the other members of the Special Forces wore ordinary caps. I never saw them answer to anyone else for their actions, but the first time when I was brought in for a second time and beaten at the police station, I was interrogated by those members of the Special Forces and beaten by them. Whereas I was not beaten by members of the Serbian police. However, we were guarded at the camp by members of the Serb police, or rather, in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one brief question in respect of the next document, and that is extract from the minutes of the 46th session of the Crisis Staff held on 29 June 1992. Witness, you'll see on the agenda, at number 2, it's marked "tasks for members of the Crisis Staff," and you'll see the third paragraph from the bottom, it states: "Momcilo K and Nedjo Dj were given the task of finding appropriate premises for the accommodation of persons who have been arrested." Could you assist the Court by telling them who you knew in the Serbian authorities who had names consistent with the first name, Momcilo, and the first initial of the surname K, and the first name Nedjo, and the first initial of the surname Dj.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 144
utterances.text: I know of only one Momcilo, Momcilo Komljenovic. I know of no other Momcilo in Kotor Varos whose family name starts with a K. It can therefore only be Momcilo Komljenovic. The second person, Nedjo Dj, from among the Serbian leaders, it can be Nedjo Djekanovic. I know of only one other Nedjo Dj. That is Nedjo Djukic, who was one of the guards at the camp where I was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 144.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour. That completes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a witness from Vlasenica, named Hasim Ferhatovic, with the code of KRAJ 175. This witness describes killings and beatings of detainees and forced labour at Susica detention camp, which was a former JNA facility. He also describes beatings and forced labour at Batkovic camp. The witness was detained in a hangar at Susica from 2 June 1992 to 30 June 1992. The camp commander was Dragan Nikolic. The witness's wife and children were also detained at Susica. The women were released after they signed a book to confirm that they were leaving Vlasenica of their own free will. Those women who refused to sign the book were threatened with beating or death unless they signed. The witness's wife and daughter were forced to surrender their valuables, including their earrings. On the night of 12 June 1992, the witness saw Nikolic and other guards beat two old prisoners with a shovel and a police baton and kick them. The witness was told to bring the two prisoners inside after they had been beaten. One of the prisoners, bleeding from his mouth and ears, died, lying next to the witness, about 40 minutes later. The witness was sent to bury the dead man and was ordered to tell the dead man's wife that he had died of a heart attack. The other prisoner was alive, but his eyes were swollen shut and his entire body was swollen. He suffered from delirium and survived in this state for about 12 hours before he too died. On the night of 23 June 1992, two other prisoners were called out from the hangar. The witness later heard cries of pain and gunshots. He was then ordered to go out and bring inside the hangar the bodies of the two prisoners, who were dead with gunshot wounds in their chests. A guard who then called another prisoner put him on a chair outside a guardhouse and then shot him repeatedly, killing him. Nikolic was drunk, on a couch, inside the guardhouse at the time. Serb police arrived following a call that prisoners had attempted to escape. When the Serb police demanded to know who had escaped, one of the prisoners lifted his head. That prisoner was taken outside. The witness later heard one shot and found the prisoner's body the following day with a single bullet hole in the centre of his forehead. The witness was forced to bury the bodies of the prisoners whose deaths are described above. He describes several other beatings of prisoners by Nikolic and camp guards. After his detention at Susica, the witness was detained for 13 months in Batkovic. He describes the beatings and gross mistreatment to which he was subjected during his detention there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this refers to the municipality of Vlasenica. This witness describes the quality of life and good inter-ethnic relationships in the village of Drum in Vlasenica municipality before 1992. In April 1992 he noted the arrival in the municipality of troops of the JNA Novi Sad Corps. He says that Serb police came to Drum in early May 1992, confiscating hunting rifles held by Muslims and calling over megaphones that if Muslims did not hand over weapons their homes would be burnt down. On 2 June 1992, the witness saw heavily armed men in military uniforms, lying in grass around the village. An APC arrived and a soldier on the APC opened fire. Soldiers emerged from both sides of the road and started to go through the village, kicking doors in and dragging people out. The witness describes several separate incidents, where he saw soldiers fire bursts of machine-gun fire into villagers. The witness recognised one of the soldiers as a Serb woman who worked in a local factory. She allowed him to leave the village in a bus filled with women, children, and two old men. From the bus, the witness saw 20 bodies of villagers killed in the attack on Drum, and he names ten of those villagers. The witness says that he recognised several of the soldiers as employees of the local bauxite mine. The witness was driven to Susica camp just outside Vlasenica town, where he was put in a warehouse with 1.000 other detainees. He says that he overheard one soldier ask another if Vlasenica had been cleaned, and the other replied in the affirmative. During the first three days at Susica, there was only some water and no food. The single toilet in the warehouse was soon overflowing. He says that the camp commander was Veljko Basic, who was replaced after the first three days by Dragan Nikolic. He describes abuse of detainees at the camp. After three days, men from Vlasenica municipality came to issue permits to those detainees who agreed to sign a statement saying that they were leaving the municipality voluntarily. 800 detainees signed, were loaded onto buses and driven away. That concludes the summary of KRAJ 178, Your Honour.
